source: Danziger, Levav, Avnaim-Pesso (2011) Extraneous factors in judicial decisions
finding: Israeli parole boards: favorable rulings fall within each of three daily sessions and jump back after each of two food breaks.
numbers: 1,112 rulings, 50 days over 10 months, 8 judges (2 female), 2 boards covering about 40% of Israeli parole requests. Favorable rate falls from about 65% to nearly 0 within a session and returns to about 65% after a break. 64.2% of requests rejected overall.
quote: justice is what the judge ate for breakfast
limits: Observational, not an experiment. Authors say they cannot test food directly. Order assumed exogenous.
agent_relevance: Shows the pattern a guardrail must watch for: later items in a long run get the default answer. Needs controls, not belief.

source: Danziger et al. (2011) case mix and daily workload
finding: Judges decide 14 to 35 cases a day, about 6 minutes each. Meal breaks fall after about 7.8 cases (morning) and 11.4 cases (late session).
numbers: Mean 22.58 cases per day (SD 4.67); mean deliberation 5.98 min (SD 5.13, max 40). Snack break mean 38.5 min, lunch mean 57.4 min. Mean judge experience 22.5 years.
limits: Break timing set by judge; session lengths unequal so late positions have few cases (plot uses first 95% of data).
agent_relevance: Sessions are long runs of repeated judgments; a scaffold can cap run length per context.

source: Danziger et al. (2011) regression with controls
finding: Logistic regression with judge fixed effects: later position lowers favorable odds and first cases after a break are higher, with legal controls in.
numbers: Overall decision count coefficient -0.078 (SE 0.020, p<0.01) in spec 1; -0.111 (SE 0.018) when counting non-decisions. Session1/decision2 dummy 1.366 (SE 0.383). Controls: crime gravity, months served, previous incarcerations, rehab program, sex, nationality, share favorable so far.
limits: Only prior incarcerations and rehab program consistently predicted rulings. No data on in-prison behaviour or on legal representation (added later in the reply).
agent_relevance: Coefficients are log odds per case. An effect-size check against lab effects is needed.

source: Danziger et al. (2011) mechanism evidence: depletion by deciding, not time
finding: Authors read the pattern as mental depletion that pushes judges to the status quo (reject). Favorable rulings take longer and have longer written verdicts.
numbers: Favorable ruling M=7.37 min (SD 5.11) vs unfavorable 5.21 (SD 4.97), t=6.86. Verdict length 89.61 words (SD 65.46) vs 47.36 (SD 43.99), t=12.82. Ordinal position and cumulative minutes correlate r=0.72; with both entered only ordinal position stays significant.
limits: The duration difference is the same fact Glockner later uses for the artifact explanation. Delays (48.4% of rejects) are lumped with rejections.
agent_relevance: Rejecting is the cheap default. An agent may drift to defaults late in long chains; test for position effects in our logs.

source: Weinshall-Margel and Shapard (2011) Overlooked factors in the analysis of parole decisions
finding: Letter: case order is not random. Unrepresented prisoners usually go last and lose more often; the board finishes one prison before a break.
numbers: Own data: 12 hearing days, n=227 decisions, plus interviews with 3 attorneys, a panel judge and 5 staff. Unrepresented prisoners about one-third of cases and win 15%; represented win 35%. Excluding deferrals: 67% vs 39%. Danziger data excluding deferrals: success about 75% falling to 42%. 4.1 prisoners per day had shared counsel.
quote: The phenomenon of favorable decisions peaking after a meal break is likely an artifact of the order of case presentation.
limits: Their own data lacked case order, so they could not rerun the test. Panel is three members, not a single judge.
agent_relevance: Case order can be confounded with case strength. An audit must randomise order, not just control for it.

source: Danziger, Levav, Avnaim-Pesso (2011) Reply to Weinshall-Margel and Shapard
finding: Authors add representation as a predictor and rerun all models; order and break effects stay.
numbers: Counsel always positively related to release but not significant in every model. Without deferrals but with representation, order and meal break remain robust. 39 cases where one attorney held two prisoners the same day, 4 with three; under one shared-counsel case per day on average. Prison-of-origin data for 5 days: same prison before and after a break.
quote: It is mathematically impossible to observe the spikes in favorable decisions after meal times in a sequence that averages approximately 22 cases.
limits: Does not report whether the effect size stayed the same. Does not address time management or selective dropout.
agent_relevance: Shows how an observational claim is defended and where it stays open.

source: Glockner (2016) The irrational hungry judge effect revisited
finding: A simulation of a rational, unbiased judge reproduces a drop of similar shape and size, because favorable rulings take longer and judges avoid starting long cases before a break.
numbers: Favorable rulings take 7.37 vs 5.21 min. In the simulation, with 5 min left only 12% of favorable cases fit vs 46% of unfavorable; favorable share falls from base rate 36% toward zero. Holds for normal and Weibull decision times. Censoring the last 5% of cases per session and autocorrelation inflate it further.
quote: an effect of similar magnitude would be produced by a (hypothetical) rational judge
limits: Shows an artifact is sufficient, not that the true effect is zero. Needs real data on planning.
agent_relevance: Computational model of the subfield. Rule: before calling an order effect a bias, simulate a rational agent under the same stopping rule.

source: Glockner (2016) effect size benchmarks
finding: The reported drop equals odds ratio 35 or d about 1.96, far above depletion effects in the lab.
numbers: 65% to 5% = OR 35, d=1.96. Depletion meta-analysis d=-0.10 to 0.25 after bias correction (Carter and McCullough 2013). Multi-lab registered replication of depletion, 23 labs, N=2,142, d=0.04 (Hagger and Chatzisarantis 2016).
limits: Depletion numbers are cited by Glockner, originals not read. Real settings could have stronger depletion than the lab.
agent_relevance: Use effect-size plausibility as a first filter on any reported bias.

source: Glockner (2016) summary of the criticism chain
finding: Lists the critiques: non-random order, selective dropout, break timing, planning. Notes the paper is cited in psychology, law and economics.
numbers: DLA censor the last 5% of cases per session; 10 to 13 cases are plotted per session; sessions range from 2 to 28 cases.
limits: Secondary summary of the dispute.
agent_relevance: Cite the dispute, not the headline.

source: Lakens (2017) Impossibly hungry judges
finding: Argues the effect is too large to be caused by a psychological mechanism.
numbers: Compares d about 2 with the 13 cm male-female height gap in the Netherlands (d=2). Law-psychology effects near d=2 in Richard, Bond, Stokes-Zoota (2003) are near-tautologies: r=0.63 (d=1.62) for majority-initial verdict. Largest in that database r=.75 (d=2.26) for ratings being reliable.
limits: Blog post, not peer reviewed. Argument is plausibility, not re-analysis.
agent_relevance: A large reported effect from a soft mechanism is a warning sign, not strength.

source: Chatziathanasiou (2022) Beware the lure of narratives
finding: Review: the hungry judge study is shaky and is wrongly used to argue for AI in law. Kahneman was the prearranged PNAS editor and featured it in Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011).
numbers: Google Scholar counted 1,415 citations on 27 Oct 2021. Summarises Weinshall-Margel and Shapard, Glockner, Lakens and the DLA reply. Points to Spamann (2020) finding no weather effect on judges.
limits: Legal scholar, argues from the literature, no new data. Spamann paper not opened.
agent_relevance: Warns against using an inflated human-bias story to justify AI; the baseline matters.

source: Chen, Moskowitz, Shue (2016) Decision-making under the gambler's fallacy
finding: Real decisions are negatively autocorrelated: a judge who just approved asylum is more likely to deny the next case, with case quality controlled.
numbers: Asylum judges: up to 3.3 percentage points more likely to deny after approving; about 2% of decisions reversed due to sequencing. Loan officers (field experiment, randomised order): up to 9% of decisions reversed for moderate officers under flat pay. MLB umpires: 1.5 percentage points less likely to call strike after a strike, more than double near the zone edge.
limits: Cannot rule out sequential contrast. Asylum data cannot show which decision was right.
agent_relevance: Strongest design in the area (randomised order in the loan setting). Gives a second order effect: contrast with the previous item, not tiredness.

source: Chen et al. (2016) boundary conditions
finding: Effect is larger for moderate decision-makers, after streaks, for similar adjacent cases, and with weak pay for accuracy. Experience reduces it.
numbers: Stronger incentive schemes cut it in the loan field experiment. A same-direction streak of two raises it.
limits: Moderators come from the authors' own tests.
agent_relevance: Anti-streak rule: do not let the previous answer set the next one; judge each item in a fresh context.

source: Chen et al. (2016) mechanism tests: gambler's fallacy vs quotas
finding: Evidence fits the law of small numbers; quotas, learning and fairness norms fit less well.
numbers: Asylum cases are randomly assigned within a court and decided first-in-first-out; they control for other judges' recent grant rates.
limits: Sequential contrast not excluded.
agent_relevance: Separate what the scaffold sees now from what it answered before.

source: Eren and Mocan (2018) Emotional judges and unlucky juveniles
finding: After an upset loss by the local college football team, Louisiana juvenile judges give longer sentences the next week.
numbers: All juvenile court decisions 1996 to 2012. Upset loss adds about 35 days, 7% of the 513-day mean. Upset wins and close losses: no effect. Placebo with other teams' games: none. Driven by judges who got their degree at LSU. Burden falls on black defendants. Small attorney-free subsample n=1,314.
limits: Observational with a point-spread design; one state. Effect confined to fans.
agent_relevance: Occasion noise from outside the case. An agent has no mood but does have context contamination.

source: Kahneman, Sibony, Sunstein (2021) Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (via Wikipedia summary)
finding: Noise is unwanted variability in judgments of the same case. Error splits into bias and noise; noise often exceeds bias.
numbers: Level noise, stable pattern noise, occasion noise. Typical order: stable pattern noise larger than occasion noise and often larger than level noise; asylum is an exception with mostly level noise.
quote: undesirable variability in judgments of the same problem
limits: I read a secondary summary, not the book.
agent_relevance: Gives a measurable quantity: variance across runs on the same item.

source: Clancy et al. (1981) sentencing study (as cited in the Noise summary)
finding: 208 criminal judges sentenced 16 fictive cases independently and varied widely.
numbers: Judges unanimously recommended prison in only 3 of 16 cases. One case: average recommendation 1.1 years, one judge recommended 15 years.
limits: Cited by a secondary page; original not opened.
agent_relevance: Direct template for an agent noise audit: same fictive case, many independent runs.

source: Noise book examples of non-judicial noise and occasion effects (as summarised)
finding: Insurance, psychiatry, courts and admissions show the same unwanted spread.
numbers: Underwriters' premiums for the same five customers varied 55%. Two psychiatrists agreed in half of 426 diagnoses. French judges more lenient on defendants' birthdays (Chen and Philippe 2020). 682 admissions decisions weighted academics more on cloudy days (Simonsohn 2007). Radiology false-positive rates 1% to 64%.
limits: Secondary summary; several are single studies.
agent_relevance: Occasion noise exists in many roles; supports an ensemble and decision hygiene.

source: Noise audit procedure and the error argument (as summarised)
finding: Noise audit: carefully prepared fictive cases, independent anonymous decisions, noise computed; optional confidence ratings.
numbers: Reducing noise by a given amount cuts total error as much as reducing bias by the same amount.
limits: Summary only.
agent_relevance: Matches our G4 (samples from one model are not independent): measure the spread before trusting the mean.

source: Englich, Mussweiler, Strack (2006) Playing dice with criminal sentences
finding: Experienced judges and prosecutors were pulled by irrelevant anchors, including a dice roll.
numbers: Not opened. Recalled from memory, unverified: dice anchor (3 vs 9) moved sentences by about 2.5 months.
limits: Publisher blocked; numbers unverified.
agent_relevance: Anchoring is the main input bias for an agent that reads a demand or prior number first.

source: Tversky and Kahneman (1974) Judgment under uncertainty
finding: Wheel-of-fortune anchor shifted estimates of the share of African nations in the UN.
numbers: Wheel at 10 gave mean 25%; wheel at 65 gave mean 45% (figures seen in a Wikipedia summary; original not opened).
limits: Original not opened. Two explanations: insufficient adjustment and selective accessibility.
agent_relevance: Use a blind first estimate and hide numbers until the agent has its own.

source: Wikipedia anchoring page, note on Ioannidis et al. (2020)
finding: The page notes a random-anchor die-roll study by Ioannidis et al. (2020) that failed to replicate anchoring effects.
numbers: No numbers on the page.
limits: Secondary and brief; original not opened.
agent_relevance: Random-number anchoring is less solid than the textbook story; relevant anchors differ from random ones.

source: Wikipedia Hungry judge effect page: later work
finding: Lists Plonsky et al. (2023) on case-order lenience via comparison direction and Haruvy et al. (2018) on fasting going opposite to prediction. Original has about 2,446 Google Scholar citations by 2026.
numbers: No figures on the page for the later studies.
limits: Secondary; neither paper opened.
agent_relevance: No clean direct replication of the meal-break effect is listed there.

source: Law and psychology must think critically about effect sizes (2023)
finding: Uses the hungry judge study as a case for critical reading of effect sizes; says the authors did not report how far effects changed with more controls.
numbers: Searched by keyword only; no new data.
limits: Skimmed, lower confidence.
agent_relevance: Report effect sizes and how they move under controls.

source: Danziger et al. (2011) why order is treated as exogenous
finding: Judge sets break timing and does not know upcoming cases; case order follows attorney arrival time. This is why the authors treat order as unrelated to merit.
numbers: Case type just ruled on had no effect on break timing (Table S15, not opened).
limits: Weinshall-Margel interviews contradict this for shared-counsel ordering.
agent_relevance: Exogeneity claims must be verifiable.

source: Danziger et al. (2011) robustness across judges
finding: No ethnicity effect on rulings; every judge showed higher favorable rates at session start than at end.
numbers: Results unchanged when dropping each judge in turn (Tables S3 to S10, not opened) and when only parole requests are kept (Table S1).
limits: Only 8 judges.
agent_relevance: Leave-one-out on the unit is a cheap test to copy.
